lesson.title: The ideal transformer: turns, volts and amps

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the primary's current rise to 6.01 A when you drag the load from 10 Ω to 5 Ω. It cancels the secondary's 5290 ampere-turns. The flux stays at 1.88 mWb.
interactive.title: The turns ratio
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Thirteen small screens on one picture, with Back and Continue. Five show an idea and eight ask you to try it. No marks and no timers.

The picture. A square iron core, as in the last two lessons, with two windings and no wire between them. The primary, on the left, sits on a 440 V, 60 Hz supply, say. The secondary, on the right, feeds a load resistor behind an open switch. Each winding is drawn longer for more turns, with its turns in a label. Beside each, a tag shows one turn and its volts per turn, 440 ÷ N1, the same on both. A voltage column beside each stacks those volts, so its height is turns × volts per turn. A flux bar runs along the core.

The controls, each shown only where a screen uses it. A primary turns slider runs from 440 to 1320 in steps of 220, opening at 880. A secondary turns slider runs from 115 to 920 in steps of 115, opening at 230. A load switch opens off. A load slider runs from 2 to 20 Ω in steps of 1, opening at 5.

The rules. Volts per turn = 440 ÷ N1, so 0.5 V at 880 turns. V2 = N2 × volts per turn, so 115 V at 230 turns. The peak flux is the last lesson's Φm = 440 ÷ (4.44 × 60 × N1): 1.88 mWb at 880 turns and 1.50 mWb at 1100. Nothing on the secondary side enters it. With the switch closed, I2 = V2 ÷ R, so 23 A on 5 Ω. The primary's current cancels the secondary's ampere-turns: I1 = N2 × I2 ÷ N1, so 6.01 A.

The readouts, which wrap onto two rows on a phone: Secondary volts, in V; Secondary current, in A, two decimal places; Primary current, in A, two decimal places. Under them: primary and secondary current bars on one scale. Two power bars, Power in = 440 × I1 and Power out = V2 × I2, in W, always equal: 2645 W on 5 Ω. An ampere-turns line, Primary N1 × I1 and Secondary N2 × I2, in At, which balance at 5290 At each on 5 Ω; its two halves wrap onto two rows on a phone. A box, As the 440 V side sees it: 440 ÷ I1 in Ω, one decimal place, which equals R × (N1 ÷ N2)². It reads 73.2 Ω on 5 Ω, and Open with the switch open. The flux bar's readout is in mWb, two decimal places. Each screen fixes the current and power bars' scales as it opens, from its turns and its heaviest load. So a bigger current always draws a longer bar. A current past the scale stops at the end of its track, with an arrow.

Screen 1, try it, a recall, typed. The picture: switch open, 880 and 230 turns. "A load has an impedance of 3 + j4 Ω. What is its size?" A typed field in Ω, whole numbers: answer 5, want "5 Ω". Slips: 7, "That adds the parts. The size is the square root of 3² + 4²."; 25, "That is 3² + 4². Now take its square root." Hint for any other answer: "Size = √(3² + 4²)." Why: "√(9 + 16) = √25 = 5 Ω. You will meet this load again later, seen through a transformer." A right Check says "Still there." and carries on. Read: "A load has an impedance of 3 + j4 Ω. What is its size?"

Screen 2, show. The secondary turns slider to drag. The words: "The volts follow the turns. One iron core carries two windings, with no wire between them. The primary has 880 turns on 440 V. The secondary has 230. The same flux threads every turn of both. So both windings get the same volts per turn. Here it is 440 ÷ 880 = 0.5 V. The secondary's 230 turns add up to 230 × 0.5 = 115 V. Drag the secondary's turns, and each one adds another 0.5 V. So V2 ÷ V1 = N2 ÷ N1.[^1]" Read: "Two windings share one core and one flux. On 440 V, the primary's 880 turns give 0.5 V per turn. So the secondary's 230 turns give 115 V. The volts follow the turns." Still: switch open, 880 and 230 turns, both voltage columns drawn.

Screen 3, try it, typed. "A primary of 880 turns sits on 440 V. A control circuit needs 24 V. How many turns does its secondary need?" A typed field in turns, whole numbers: answer 48, want "48 turns". Slips: 12, "That multiplies 24 by 0.5. Each turn gives 0.5 V, so divide."; 37, "That is 880 ÷ 24. Find the volts per turn first." Hint for any other answer: "Volts per turn = 440 ÷ 880. Then divide 24 V by it." Why: "440 ÷ 880 = 0.5 V per turn. 24 ÷ 0.5 = 48 turns. Check: 48 turns × 0.5 V = 24 V." Read: "A primary of 880 turns sits on 440 V. A control circuit needs 24 V. How many turns does its secondary need?"

Screen 4, show. The load switch to close. The words: "The primary cancels the secondary's ampere-turns. Close the load switch. A 5 Ω load on 115 V draws 23 A. The secondary's 230 turns now carry 230 × 23 = 5290 ampere-turns. They push against the change that made them. But the flux must still make 440 V in the primary, to match the supply. So it cannot shrink. Instead, the primary draws 5290 ÷ 880 = 6.01 A extra to cancel them. The ampere-turns balance: N1 × I1 = N2 × I2. Fewer turns carry more amps." Read: "With a 5 Ω load, the secondary's 230 turns carry 23 A. That is 5290 ampere-turns. The primary cancels them with 6.01 A through its 880 turns." Still: switch closed, 5 Ω.

Screen 5, try it, typed. "A 440 V to 115 V transformer supplies 40 A on its 115 V side. What current does its 440 V side take?" A typed field in A, two decimal places: answer 10.45, want "10.45 A". Slips: 153.04, "That makes the 115 V side's current the smaller. A step-down raises the current, so the 440 V side carries less."; 40, "The two currents differ by the same ratio as the volts." Hint for any other answer: "I1 = I2 × 115 ÷ 440." Why: "The volts step down by 440 ÷ 115 = 3.826. So the amps step up by the same. 40 ÷ 3.826 = 10.45 A. Check: 440 × 10.45 and 115 × 40 both come to about 4600 W." Read: "A 440 V to 115 V transformer supplies 40 A on its 115 V side. What current does its 440 V side take?"

Screen 6, show. All three sliders to drag. The words: "Power in equals power out. Watch the two power bars. Power in is 440 V times 6.01 A. Power out is 115 V times 23 A. Both come to 2645 W. Drag the load or either winding's turns, and they stay equal. The volts step down by the turns ratio. The amps step up by the same ratio. So volts times amps is the same on both sides. The transformer passes power on. Ideally, it makes none and uses none." Read: "Power in is 440 V times 6.01 A. Power out is 115 V times 23 A. Both come to 2645 W, and they stay equal at every setting." Still: switch closed, 5 Ω, 880 and 230 turns.

Screen 7, try it, typed. "A 440 V to 115 V transformer feeds a 3 kW heater on its 115 V side. What current does it take from the 440 V supply?" A typed field in A, two decimal places: answer 6.82, want "6.82 A". Slips: 26.09, "That is the heater's own current, at 115 V. The 440 V side takes less."; 0.01, "That uses 3 W. A kilowatt is 1000 W." Hint for any other answer: "Power in equals power out. So I1 = 3000 ÷ 440." Why: "Power in equals power out, which is 3000 W. 3000 ÷ 440 = 6.82 A. The heater itself takes 3000 ÷ 115 = 26.09 A." Read: "A 440 V to 115 V transformer feeds a 3 kW heater on its 115 V side. What current does it take from the 440 V supply?"

Screen 8, show. The load and primary turns sliders to drag. The words: "The load does not move the flux. Watch the flux bar as you drag the load. It stays at 1.88 mWb. The flux must still make 440 V in the primary, so it swings the same. The primary cancels every ampere-turn the load adds. So a heavier load does not push the core towards saturation. In this ideal picture, only the supply's voltage, its frequency or the primary's turns move the flux. Drag the primary to 1100 turns, and the flux falls to 1.50 mWb." Read: "The flux stays at 1.88 mWb at every load. It moves only with the supply or the primary's turns. On 1100 turns, it falls to 1.50 mWb." Still: switch closed, 2 Ω, 880 turns.

Screen 9, try it, typed. "A 440 V, 60 Hz supply feeds a primary of 880 turns. The load changes from 10 Ω to 5 Ω, and the secondary current doubles from 11.5 A to 23 A. What is the peak flux now?" A typed field in mWb, two decimal places: answer 1.88, want "1.88 mWb". The flux readout shows ? until Check. Slips: 3.76, "That doubles the flux with the load. The primary cancels the extra ampere-turns."; 0.94, "That halves it. The load does not move the flux either way." Hint for any other answer: "Φm = V ÷ (4.44 × f × N1). Is the load in it?" Why: "Φm = 440 ÷ (4.44 × 60 × 880) = 1.88 mWb. The load is not in the rule, so the flux stays put. The primary's current rises from 3.01 A to 6.01 A. That cancels the extra ampere-turns." A right Check moves the load from 10 Ω to 5 Ω with the switch closed. Read: "A 440 V, 60 Hz supply feeds a primary of 880 turns. The load changes from 10 Ω to 5 Ω, and the secondary current doubles from 11.5 A to 23 A. What is the peak flux now?"

Screen 10, show. The load slider to drag. The words: "Seen from the supply, the load looks bigger by the turns ratio squared. The supply sees only its own 440 V and the 6.01 A it gives. So the load looks like 440 ÷ 6.01 = 73.2 Ω. The box shows it. On this side, the volts are 3.83 times higher. The amps are 3.83 times lower. So the load looks bigger by the ratio twice over: 5 × (880 ÷ 230)² = 5 × 14.64 = 73.2 Ω. Drag the load, and the box stays at 14.64 times it." Read: "The 440 V side sees 440 V driving 6.01 A. That looks like 73.2 Ω. It is the 5 Ω load times (880 ÷ 230)², which is 14.64." Still: switch closed, 5 Ω.

Screen 11, try it, typed. "On the same 880 to 230 turn transformer, the load is 2.5 Ω. What resistance does the 440 V side see?" A typed field in Ω, one decimal place: answer 36.6, want "36.6 Ω". The box shows ? until Check. Slips: 9.6, "That multiplies by the ratio once. Volts and amps each change, so square it."; 0.2, "That divides. Seen from the higher voltage, the load looks bigger." Hint for any other answer: "Seen resistance = load × (N1 ÷ N2)²." Why: "(880 ÷ 230)² = 14.64. So the 440 V side sees 2.5 × 14.64 = 36.6 Ω. Check: 115 V on 2.5 Ω draws 46 A. The primary takes 46 × 230 ÷ 880 = 12.02 A. And 440 ÷ 12.02 = 36.6 Ω." A right Check sets the load to 2.5 Ω. Read: "On the same 880 to 230 turn transformer, the load is 2.5 Ω. What resistance does the 440 V side see?"

Screen 12, try it, the first of two mixed puzzles. "The load on the 115 V side is 3 + j4 Ω. You found its size at the start. The transformer has 880 and 230 turns. What impedance does the 440 V side see?" Four choices, in this order: "3 + j4 Ω"; "11.5 + j15.3 Ω"; "43.9 + j58.6 Ω"; "73.2 + j0 Ω". Right, the third. Hint for the first: "From the other side, the load looks bigger by the ratio squared." Hint for the second: "That scales it by the ratio once. It takes the ratio squared." Hint for the fourth: "73.2 Ω is its size. Scaling by a plain number keeps its angle." Why: "The ratio squared, 14.64, is a plain number. It scales both parts: 3 × 14.64 = 43.9 and 4 × 14.64 = 58.6. The size grows from 5 Ω to 73.2 Ω. The angle stays the same. So the power factor is the same from both sides." Read: "A 3 + j4 Ω load sits on the 115 V side of the 880 to 230 turn transformer. What impedance does the 440 V side see?"

Screen 13, try it, the second mixed puzzle, typed. "A small step-up transformer has 200 turns on 115 V. Its secondary has 800 turns and feeds 2.3 A. What current does the primary take?" The picture: a step-up, 440 and 920 turns on 20 Ω, so the I1 bar is the longer. A typed field in A, one decimal place: answer 9.2, want "9.2 A". Slips: 0.6, "That has the current rising with the volts. The higher-voltage side carries less, so turn it round."; 2.3, "The two currents differ by the turns ratio." Hint for any other answer: "N1 × I1 = N2 × I2." Why: "800 × 2.3 = 1840 ampere-turns. The primary must cancel them, so it takes 1840 ÷ 200 = 9.2 A. Check the power. The secondary gives 115 × 800 ÷ 200 = 460 V. 460 × 2.3 and 115 × 9.2 both come to 1058 W." Read: "A step-up transformer has 200 turns on 115 V. Its secondary has 800 turns and feeds 2.3 A. What current does the primary take?"

The finish. The words: "Every turn on one core gets the same volts, so the volts follow the turns. The primary cancels the secondary's ampere-turns, so the amps go the other way. Power in equals power out. The flux stays where the supply holds it. Seen through the windings, a load scales by the turns ratio squared. That lets you draw a transformer and its load as one circuit. Next: the real transformer, and where its watts go."

Every figure on these screens is an example value or worked from the rules above.
interactive.ignores: The transformer is ideal. It draws no current to make its flux. So with the switch open, the primary current reads 0 A. A real one draws a small magnetising current even at no load. Every line of flux is drawn through both windings. In a real core a little leaks round each winding. The windings have no resistance, and the core has no loss. So power in exactly equals power out. The secondary voltage holds at every load. A real transformer warms up, loses a little power, and its output sags a little under load. Under load its flux also falls a very little. The load is a pure resistance on a single-phase supply. Every current and voltage is rms. The core never saturates. The windings are drawn far shorter than real ones.

explain.text:
In a transformer, both windings share one flux. So every turn gets the same voltage, and the volts follow the turns. The supply holds that flux, so a load barely moves it. Whatever ampere-turns the secondary draws, the primary cancels with its own. So the amps go the other way, and power in equals power out.

Each turn gets an emf set by how fast the flux through it changes. Picture an [[ideal transformer]]. All its flux stays in the core. So the same flux threads every turn of both windings. Then every turn gets the same volts. On 440 V, a primary of 880 turns has 0.5 V per turn. A secondary of 230 turns adds up 230 of them. That makes 115 V. So V2 ÷ V1 = N2 ÷ N1.[^1] In a two-winding transformer like this one, the windings share only the flux. No wire joins them. So the secondary is a circuit of its own.

Now switch a 5 Ω load onto the secondary. It draws 115 ÷ 5 = 23 A. So its 230 turns carry 5290 ampere-turns. By Lenz's law, they push against the change that made them. On their own they would shrink the flux. But the flux must still make 440 V in the primary, to match the supply. So the primary draws just enough extra current to cancel them. That is 5290 ÷ 880 = 6.01 A. This is the [[ampere-turn balance]]: N1 × I1 = N2 × I2. A step-down transformer's secondary has fewer turns, so it carries more current, not less. Multiply volts by amps on each side, and both give 2645 W. The transformer passes power on. Ideally, it makes none and uses none.

The supply sees only its 440 V and the 6.01 A it gives. So to the supply, the 5 Ω load looks like 440 ÷ 6.01 = 73.2 Ω. On this side, the volts are higher by the turns ratio. The amps are lower by it. So the load looks bigger by the ratio squared: 5 × (880 ÷ 230)² = 73.2 Ω. This is the load's [[reflected impedance]]. It lets you draw the whole transformer and its load as one circuit, on one side. This picture is simplified. A real transformer needs a small magnetising current. It loses a little power, as little as 1% in a good one.[^2] And its output sags a little under load. **In an ideal transformer the volts follow the turns, the amps go the other way, and power in equals power out.**

analogy.text: Think of two meshed gears in a gearbox. Where the teeth meet, each tooth pushes on the other with the same force. So each gear's torque follows its teeth. In the same way, each winding's volts follow its turns. The gear with more teeth turns slower. Likewise, the winding with more turns carries less current. Torque times speed is the same on both shafts, less a little friction. Volts times amps is the same on both windings.
analogy.breaks: A gearbox holds a steady torque with its shafts still. A transformer passes nothing on steady DC. Its flux must keep changing. Metal teeth join two gears. In a two-winding transformer, only the flux joins the windings. So the secondary is a separate circuit.

practice.text:
- Treat a secondary as live whenever its primary is energised. Its full voltage is there with no load at all.
- Find the turns ratio, N1 ÷ N2. In an ideal transformer, it equals V1 ÷ V2. For 440 V to 115 V, it is 3.83.
- Volts: V2 = V1 × N2 ÷ N1.
- Amps: I1 = I2 × N2 ÷ N1. On a step-down transformer, the secondary carries the larger current.
- Check the power: V1 × I1 should match V2 × I2. A real transformer gives out a little less than it takes in.
- To see a load from the primary side, multiply its impedance by (N1 ÷ N2)². To move one from the primary side to the secondary side, divide by it.
- Size each side's cables and protection for that side's own current.

**Rules of thumb:** Volts go with the turns. Amps go against them. Volts times amps stays the same. The supply sets the flux, not the load.

**Worked example:** A single-phase 10 kVA transformer steps 440 V down to 115 V. It is rated in kVA, not kW, because its losses follow the volts and the amps, whatever the power factor. Its turns ratio is 440 ÷ 115 = 3.83. At full load, the 440 V side takes 10,000 ÷ 440 = 22.7 A. The 115 V side gives 10,000 ÷ 115 = 87.0 A. Check: 87.0 ÷ 22.7 = 3.83. That is the turns ratio again. From the 440 V side, a 5 Ω load on the 115 V side looks like 5 × (440 ÷ 115)² = 73.2 Ω.

**Common mistakes**
- Thinking a step-down transformer steps the current down too. It steps it up.
- Expecting a heavy load to push the core towards saturation. The supply sets the flux. The primary cancels the load's ampere-turns.
- Scaling an impedance by the ratio once. It takes the ratio squared.
- Turning the ratio upside down. Ask which side has the higher voltage. That side carries the smaller current and sees the bigger impedance.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the primary's current rise to 6.01 A when you drag the load from 10 Ω to 5 Ω. It cancels the secondary's 5290 ampere-turns. The flux stays at 1.88 mWb.

checks.label: The ratio of the secondary to primary voltages equals the ratio of the turns in their windings
The same flux permeates each turn of both the primary and the secondary, so each turn carries the same volts on both sides
The current ratio is the inverse of the voltage ratio, and the transformer neither creates nor consumes power
On 5 Ω the secondary draws 23 A, so 5290 ampere-turns; the primary cancels them with 6.01 A, and 2645 W goes in and out
The flux holds at 1.88 mWb with the switch open and on 10, 5 or 2 Ω, and falls to 1.50 mWb on 1100 primary turns
A step-down raises the current: on 880 and 230 turns the secondary current bar is 3.83 times the primary's; on 660 and 920 turns, and in the step-up puzzle's picture, it is the shorter
A bigger current always draws a longer bar: on 10 Ω, taking the secondary from 230 to 460 turns doubles the I2 bar and quadruples the power bars
The 440 V side sees 73.2 Ω on 5 Ω, which is 5 × 14.64, 146.4 Ω on 10 Ω and 29.3 Ω on 2 Ω
A right Check on the 3 kW heater moves the load to 115² ÷ 3000 = 4.41 Ω, where the primary takes 6.82 A and 3000 W goes in
Before a Check the flux and the box show ?; a right Check moves the load from 10 Ω to 5 Ω with the flux at 1.88 mWb, and from 5 Ω to 2.5 Ω with the box at 36.6 Ω
Every demonstration ends 3 to 4.5 s after its screen opens, and every answer's motion within 2.5 s

applied.problem: "A load cannot move it" is absolute: in a real transformer the flux falls a very little under load (the ignores panel says so), and later "No wire joins them" is false for the auto-transformer of i8, so both are narrowed.
"Only the flux joins two windings, so the secondary is a separate circuit" stops being true once i8 teaches the auto-transformer, whose windings share wire; narrowed to a two-winding transformer.
Screen 5's check says 440 × 10.45 comes to 4600 W, but it is 4598 W; the rounded current only gives about 4600 W, so a learner checking it by hand would be puzzled.
